title: To decipher local laws, researchers used AI to build a database of millions of them
key_facts: UC Berkeley researchers led by Diag Davenport (Goldman School of Public Policy and School of Information) built a free, open-access database of local laws from all 50 states, which the university calls the first for local laws specifically.
The team collected nearly 10,000 documents, roughly 7 million pages, many of them blurry or poorly structured PDFs, from more than 3,000 counties and about 6,000 other local jurisdictions.
A vision-language model for reading scanned pages, LightOnOCR, extracted text and structure, and OpenAI models were used to tag and organize samples of the laws.
The database holds millions of unique ordinances and lets researchers search for patterns in how communities regulate housing, public space and business.
The team put a version online in June, and some people have already built searchable interfaces on it.
A paper on the project was accepted last week at NeurIPS, to be presented in December.

Davenport says future tools built on the data, such as chatbots for specific topics, must be free and public; he says the work was not possible until six to twelve months ago and was done at a larger scale than anyone else, as far as he knows.

why_it_matters_hint: Local laws that were scattered across thousands of hard-to-search sites can now be compared in one place.
event_date: Database online June 2026 (exact date not stated); paper accepted the week before 2 Oct; release dated 2 Oct 2026
notes: Official university release. The database has been online since June and the paper acceptance was last week, so score lowered 4 to 3 (older event). 'First-of-its-kind' and 'largest' are the team's own claims. The release gives no accuracy figures for the AI tagging.
